transcript:
Header: 2025-11-18 15:00 PST | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Claire Nguyen (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (NovaCommerce - Product), Ethan Ross (NovaCommerce - ML Eng), Samira Ahmed (NovaCommerce - CTO)

[00:00] Claire: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I think we have about 40 minutes. Quick agenda: intro, quick questions about your use case, then Marcus will demo the hosted API for chat/text generation focusing on streaming, key params, and retries, and then we'll do Q&A and next steps. Sound good?

[00:18] Priya: Yep sounds great, thanks Claire. We're excited to see how Redwood could plug into our recommendations chat.

[00:26] Marcus: Awesome, thanks Priya. Real quick can you describe current stack and what success looks like?

[00:33] Priya: Sure. We have a microservices front end on GKE, all user requests through our API gateway. Right now we're calling OpenAI for prompt-based recommendations, but latency is a bit variable and cost is creeping up. Success is accurate suggestions in under 800ms p95 and predictable unit cost.

[00:52] Ethan: Also from infra, we need SSO and SOC2 posture docs for any vendor and prefer VPC peering for private instances, but for hosted we're open if data residency and encryption is clear.

[01:10] Claire: Great, that's helpful. We'll share SOC2 and security pack after the call. Marcus, over to you for the demo.

[01:15] Marcus: Cool. I'll kick off in the Console quick view then show a couple of SDK calls. First note: Redwood Hosted API supports streaming so you can render partial tokens in the UI as they arrive, it's a chunked HTTP stream or websocket. In practice the UI gets tokens progressively so users see the response quickly.

[02:02] Marcus: (screen) Here's a simple curl example for streaming - we open the stream, server sends events with token fragments and a final event. If the transcript's truncated, you might see partial words sometimes if packet boundaries fall mid-token, that's normal and client side can buffer a token buffer.

[02:34] Ethan: Quick q, does streaming increase cost vs non-streaming?

[02:39] Marcus: Good question. No direct cost delta for streaming itself, billing is by tokens generated. The tradeoff is you might surface tokens earlier so perceived latency improves, but total token usage is same. Also note we have streaming timeouts and you can tune the chunk size at the client.

[03:10] Marcus: Now parameters: temperature controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling, presence and frequency penalties help steer repeated outputs. Max_tokens caps response length; we recommend server-side truncation to protect SLAs. For chat we also offer system/user/assistant roles.

[03:45] Priya: For our recs we want stable outputs with occasional creativity - what's a good baseline?

[03:51] Marcus: Start with temperature 0.2-0.3 and top_p 0.9, presence penalty 0.0, frequency 0.5 if you see repeats. Then run evals and tune. Our Optimize recommendations can suggest quantization and batching settings once we see traffic.

[04:20] Marcus: On retries: we recommend idempotency keys for requests that could be retried. Retries should use exponential backoff with jitter; avoid blind retries for streaming sessions. If a streaming connection drops, the client should either resume (if you track state and tokens) or issue a new request with the same idempotency key and server-side dedupe will prevent duplicate side effects.

[05:05] Ethan: Do you provide automatic dedupe or is that on the client?

[05:10] Marcus: We provide idempotency token support for non-streaming and some streaming resumptions; for full dedupe semantics you should include a request id and server will check recent completions. We also expose logs so you can inspect if a duplicate request resulted in two completions.

[05:40] Samira: How about rate limits? If we spike during peak shopping, will we hit throttles?

[05:47] Claire: For Hosted there are per-account rate limits; we can configure higher quotas for customers after sizing. If you need deterministic throughput we'd talk about Dedicated. For Hosted we can set burst quotas and suggest batching on the client to smooth spikes.

[06:10] Marcus: Back to demo, here's a code snippet in Node showing streaming via the SDK: open stream, on data append tokens, on end finalize. Important: handle partial tokens and backpressure; don't render until a token boundary if that matters visually.

[06:45] Marcus: Also showing retries example: attach an idempotency key header, on 5xx do exponential backoff up to N attempts, cancel on 4xx. For long running responses consider server-sent events with a keepalive to avoid intermediate timeouts.

[07:20] Priya: Are there client libraries that implement recommended retry/backoff patterns?

[07:25] Marcus: Yes our SDKs have built-in helpers for retry/backoff and streaming consumption patterns; we include examples for React/Node. They expose hooks to customize jitter and attempt limits.

[07:50] Ethan: About latency, what should we expect for 1-2k tokens on average?

[07:56] Marcus: Typical hosted 1-2k token responses vary by model; for smaller open models p95 might be 600-900ms, for larger ones 1.2-1.8s. We'll run a benchmark for your prompt set to get exact numbers. Also caching prefix/KV cache can cut repeated prompt costs and latency substantially.

[08:30] Priya: We use dynamic contextual prompts with user history, does Redwood support per-user caching?

[08:36] Marcus: We have prefix caching for repeated prefixes; per-user depends on how much overlap there is. Our Optimize tooling can recommend which parts to cache and batching strategies.

[09:00] Marcus: Quick aside on errors: common errors are rate_limit, context_length_exceeded, and internal_server_error. For context length, either trim history or use summarization. For rate limits, exponential backoff. For internal errors surface a friendly retry or fallback to a lighter model.

[09:35] Priya: Do you support structured response enforcement or function calls?

[09:40] Marcus: Yes, we support structured output via schemas and also function/tool calling for actions. For this demo I'm focusing on chat/text basics but we can schedule a deep dive on function calling.

[09:58] Claire: Quick security note - we'll share our SOC2 report and details on KMS integration. Hosted customers can opt into customer-managed keys in some tiers and we support TLS in transit and AES-256 at rest.

[10:15] Samira: For compliance we need audit logs retained for 1 year and role-based access. Is that possible?

[10:23] Claire: Yes audit log retention and RBAC are available; retention windows vary by plan but we can offer enterprise add-ons. We'll include specifics in the security pack.

[10:40] Marcus: Back to the console - here's the model catalog with verified performance profiles, you can pin a model version, set per-route SLOs, and enable streaming. Also console shows token-level cost per call which helps diagnose expensive prompts.

[11:10] Marcus: I'm going to demo a live streaming call. (typing) Sending a sample prompt that asks for 3 product recommendations given user context. Stream events begin to arrive... you can see the UI fills as tokens stream in. Sometimes you'll see fragments like 'recommend-' then 'ations' if boundary hits, which the client should join.

[12:00] Priya: Looks good, how do you measure tokenized cost for multi-turn chats?

[12:06] Marcus: We count input + output tokens; conversation state accumulation increases tokens, so recommended patterns are summarization or storing embeddings for history retrieval to reduce token size. Optimize can suggest quantization and batching for cost reductions.

[12:30] Ethan: For the benchmark, any specifics you need?

[12:34] Marcus: A sample of 200 representative prompts, typical concurrency (RPS), desired p95 SLOs and max budget per 1k tokens would be ideal. We'll run a 10k token end-to-end test to measure tail latency and costs.

[13:05] Priya: We can assemble that. Also curious about retries again - if a request times out and client retries, how to avoid duplicate charges?

[13:14] Marcus: If you supply an idempotency key the server can detect retries and avoid double executions within a short window; for long running completions we recommend persisting partial results server-side and returning a completion id so retries can check status rather than re-run.

[13:45] Samira: Any gotchas for streamed responses with mobile clients?

[13:49] Marcus: Mobile networks can drop connections; implement resume logic where possible and show fallback messaging. On limited bandwidth you might opt for shorter max_tokens or prefetch recommendations server-side then push to client.

[14:10] Claire: Quick commercial note - Hosted pricing is usage-based per 1k tokens; dedicated pricing available if you need committed capacity. I'll follow up with a pricing sheet.

[14:28] Priya: If we start with Hosted and later move to Dedicated, how smooth is migration?

[14:33] Marcus: We intentionally designed the API consistent across modes; you can pin model versions and rollouts transfer. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and tighter SLOs. Console supports canary and A/B rollouts so migration is manageable.

[15:00] Marcus: Wrapping up demo, quick recap: streaming available and recommended for snappy UX, tune temperature/top_p for creativity, use idempotency keys and exponential backoff to handle retries, and we'll run a benchmark with your prompts.

[15:20] Priya: Sounds good. One last question: do you support embeddings + chat in a single pipeline for retrieval-augmented generation?

[15:27] Marcus: Yes, we have embeddings endpoints and you can combine retrieval results with the chat prompt; Optimize can recommend quantization for embedding storage and caching to lower costs.

[15:40] Claire: Great. Next steps: we'll send security docs/SOC2, pricing, and Marcus will kick off the benchmark. Should we tentatively schedule the POC scoping for Nov 24?

[15:52] Priya: That works for us.

[16:00] Claire: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the items and calendar invite.

[16:07] (call wraps, informal chatter)

Notes: occasional transcription artifacts - product names sometimes transcribed as 'Redwood Optimise' or 'K-V cash'; speaker labels autoassigned in places.
